This person is a 67-year-old neighborhood association president in Boston, a retired teacher, who supports fewer people in prison but wants implementation to include zoning and siting standards for reentry housing (caps per block, 24/7 onsite staff), community benefit agreements, data sharing on outcomes, and rapid-response nuisance abatement, citing past experiences with poorly managed halfway houses concentrating impacts on one street.

This person is a 35-year-old tech product manager in Denver whose company supplies validated risk assessments and electronic monitoring, advocating that population reductions be implemented with statewide adoption of transparent, independently validated tools, open APIs for court and corrections data, pilot-to-scale pathways with outcome targets, and funding for graduated supervision, arguing these alternatives maintain safety while shrinking prison counts.

This person is a 34-year-old Latina public defender in Harris County, Texas, who wants to cut pretrial detention by eliminating cash bail for low-risk charges, guaranteeing counsel at first appearance, expanding 24/7 magistrate coverage, and scaling up mental-health and LEAD diversion with transportation and housing supports; she cares because she routinely watches indigent clients sit weeks on $500 bonds for cases that later get dismissed, derailing jobs and families.

This person is a 29-year-old Black mother in Oakland, California, formerly incarcerated on a nonviolent offense, who advocates reducing re-incarceration by capping technical parole violations, providing transitional housing vouchers, childcare-linked job training, automatic record sealing after supervision, and eliminating supervision fees; she cares because she was sent back to prison for a curfew violation and lost both housing and employment.

This person is a 63-year-old crime victim advocate in Minneapolis, Minnesota, who supports fewer people in prison if early releases include enforceable restitution plans, upgraded victim-notification systems, GPS monitoring for high-risk domestic violence cases, and restorative justice only with victim consent and trained facilitators; he cares because his sibling was assaulted and felt excluded from early-release decisions.

This person is a state prison warden in Ohio, age 54, who supports reducing the population by expanding geriatric parole eligibility to 55+, revising earned-time credits up to 20% for evidence-based vocational and cognitive behavioral programs, and sequencing facility downsizing with staff redeployment plans; they care because an aging incarcerated population has doubled medical costs and contributed to violence, and their pilot step-down unit cut serious incidents by 18% in a year.

This person is a county prosecutor in Maricopa County, age 50, who accepts targeted decarceration only if repeat violent offenses are excluded, victims are consulted before diversion, and risk tools are independently audited for racial bias with transparent release criteria; they care because case outcomes and community safety depend on credible constraints and because past unaudited tools produced inconsistent results.

This person is a formerly incarcerated father and small-business owner in Detroit, age 39, who advocates for automatic record sealing after three conviction-free years, state-funded transitional housing vouchers on release, guaranteed state ID and licensing help at the gate, and performance-based grants to employers who hire returnees; they care because a stale felony record and lack of housing blocked contracts despite full compliance and training.
